rationale: A wins because it keeps the launch inside provable lanes and turns every weakness into a reporting gate. Its strongest angle, "Airbnb builds a travel-manager console to get short-term rentals written into company policy," is a real buyer-side story with a concrete reporter, conflict, and proof test. B has good bones, but "Airbnb Moves Into Business Travel Tech, Targeting the Market Navan Built" starts importing market history the update did not give it. That is how a pitch gets dressed up, then killed in the first fact-check.
gaps_in_A: "Airbnb goes after managed corporate lodging spend with a tool it gives away" overreads "free for travelers"; the update does not prove it is free to employers, hosts, or partners.
"people who are often one-property operators" is plausible color, not supplied fact. Keep it as a question, not a premise.
"Airbnb plugs into Concur and Ramp" is journalist-shaped, but thin without partner confirmation or a customer using it; A correctly flags that, but it is still the weakest kept angle.
gaps_in_B: "Targeting the Market Navan Built" invents a competitive frame the update did not supply. Naming Navan, TravelPerk, Booking.com for Business, and hotel chains may be useful research, but it is not grounded enough for the angle headline.
"Many Won't Qualify" is a made-up conclusion. The set later asks how many hosts qualify, which proves the headline is guessing.
"the compliance gap that blocked corporate adoption" asserts causality the facts do not support. The update says expense integrations exist, not that this was the blocker.
B misses the cleanest buyer-policy angle: travel managers getting a dashboard, one bill, and expense feeds that could move Airbnb from rogue bookings into company policy.
